takeaways: Jason's five reasons Minneapolis will thrive over the next decade. First, the economy: 15 Fortune 500 headquarters, the highest per capita among the 30 largest metros, and a diverse job base where no single industry has more than about 18% of jobs.

Second, anchor institutions: the University of Minnesota (about 55,000 students on the Twin Cities campus), Medical Alley and Mayo Clinic, which is expanding in Rochester with a roughly $5 billion investment. Health care and education held up through 2008 and the pandemic.

Third, redevelopment downtown: the old Dayton's building is becoming a mixed-use landmark with a food hall, 150 South Fifth Street is being converted to about 280 apartments, and Target's former office space to about 500 apartments. The North Loop and the Upper Harbor riverfront project are reshaping the city.

Fourth, lifestyle: more than 180 parks, about 6,800 acres of parkland, the Chain of Lakes and the Grand Rounds, with 99% of residents within a 10-minute walk of a park. Minneapolis ranked second among large U.S. cities for biking in 2025.

Fifth, affordability: the city's median is in the mid-$300,000s versus the low $600,000s in Seattle and the $800,000s in Boston. As stated in the video (November 2025), Northeast ran from the low $300,000s to low $400,000s, the North Loop from the high $400,000s to low $600,000s, and Uptown from the mid-$400,000s to mid-$500,000s.
Property taxes average about 1.25% of value, below Chicago and Milwaukee, and home insurance runs about $2,000 a year versus $3,000 to $5,000 in many coastal markets, according to Jason.

faq.q: Is Minneapolis affordable compared to other big cities?
faq.a: Yes. The video puts the Minneapolis median in the mid-$300,000s, about 30% to 45% less than Boston, Seattle or Denver, with lower property tax rates than Chicago or Milwaukee.

faq.q: Are downtown Minneapolis office buildings being turned into apartments?
faq.a: Yes. Projects include 150 South Fifth Street (about 280 apartments) and Target's former downtown office space (about 500 apartments), plus the mixed-use Dayton's redevelopment.

takeaways: Seven common mistakes buyers make in Minnesota. 1: not understanding winter maintenance: snow load on the roof, ice dams from poor attic insulation and ventilation, and the cost of clearing a long driveway. Ask the sellers what they spend.
2: skipping the sewer or septic inspection. Many older Twin Cities homes have clay sewer pipes that crack and let tree roots in; a camera scope gives you a video report.

3: assuming every home is energy efficient. Homes built after about 2000 usually are; many built before about 1990 aren't, unless they've been renovated. Ask for utility bills, keeping in mind the sellers' thermostat habits.
4: ignoring flood zones. They're less common in Minnesota, but check FEMA flood maps.
5: not knowing the property taxes, which vary widely by city and district and tend to be higher inside the seven-county metro. A strong commercial tax base can help keep residential taxes down.
6: underestimating the commute, which can triple on a big snow day. 7: falling in love too fast in a competitive market; take time to think it through.

faq.q: Should I skip the sewer inspection to make my offer stronger?
faq.a: Jason says no. Many older homes have clay sewer pipes prone to cracks and root intrusion, and a camera scope costs little compared with a sewer line replacement.

Ridges of ice at the roof edge that form when heat escapes into the attic and melts snow, which then refreezes. Water can back up under the shingles and leak inside. Good attic insulation and ventilation prevent them.

takeaways: A commercial listing tour in the Fieldstone industrial park in Lakeville, about a half mile from I-35W: a new 10,000-square-foot building on about 2.5 acres, listed at $1,850,000 at the time.

It's two mirror-image 5,000-square-foot bays separated by a non-load-bearing wall that could be opened up. Each bay has two restrooms, floor drains, three 14-foot overhead doors with commercial openers, a 200-amp three-phase panel, exhaust fans and LED lighting.
The county allows generous outdoor storage, and the perimeter is paved with gravel storage behind. There's no air conditioning yet, but it could be added.
Huerkamp Home Group handles commercial as well as residential real estate.

faq.q: Does Huerkamp Home Group handle commercial property?
faq.a: Yes. Besides residential sales, the team lists and sells commercial property, like this 10,000-square-foot industrial building in Lakeville.

takeaways: A December tour of the Morgan model by Key Land Homes in Big Sky Estates, a newer neighborhood in Savage with lots still available. It's close to Highway 169 and I-35W, under 30 minutes to the airport or either downtown.
Five bedrooms, four baths and about 3,700 to 3,800 square feet, listed in the low to mid-$800,000s at the time (the model includes upgrades).

The main level has 10-foot ceilings, 8-foot solid-core doors, a large office, a navy-and-gold kitchen with quartz counters and true double ovens, an eat-in dining area (no formal dining room) and a butler's pantry with a second dishwasher and beverage fridge. A rear staircase is tucked off the mudroom.

Upstairs are a large laundry room, four bedrooms with walk-in closets (one Jack-and-Jill bath, one with its own bath) and an owner's suite with a vaulted ceiling, soaking tub and large tiled shower. The lookout lower level has 9-foot ceilings, a family room, another bedroom and a three-quarter bath.

faq.q: What does about $800,000 buy in new construction in Savage?
faq.a: In this tour, about 3,700 square feet with five bedrooms, four baths, 10-foot main-floor ceilings and a finished lower level, in the Big Sky Estates neighborhood.

takeaways: A tour of a new executive rambler by Peach Builders, a family-owned Lakeville custom builder in business for about 40 years, priced at $675,000 at the time.

One-level living: 11-foot ceilings on the main floor, custom cabinets, an office, a kitchen with double ovens and a cooktop, an eat-in dining area with a buffet, and an owner's suite with a walk-in shower and laundry next to the closet. The home faces a pond with west-facing sunset views.
The finished lower level adds a family room, a game area, a full bath, two bedrooms and lots of storage. Poured foundation walls, an air-to-air exchanger and a sump pump are included.
The three-car garage has 12-foot ceilings, 8-foot doors, floor drains and gas run for a heater, and the yard has irrigation.

faq.a: A larger one-story home with the owner's suite, kitchen, laundry and main living spaces on one floor, often with a finished lower level for guests.

takeaways: City or suburbs? By sticker price, Minneapolis looks cheaper (median in the high $300,000s versus about $400,000 in Maple Grove, the high $400,000s in Plymouth and the mid-$500,000s in Eden Prairie), but city homes tend to be older, on smaller lots and in need of updates.

A nice 1,800-square-foot downtown condo can cost about $6,000 a month all-in, which could instead cover a four-bedroom suburban home with a yard and a three-car garage, according to Jason. Effective property tax rates also differ: about 1.17% in Eden Prairie and Chanhassen versus about 0.99% in Dakota County.
Character is the city's edge: homes from about 1880 to 1930 with original woodwork. Only a few areas, like Uptown, Lyn-Lake and the North Loop, are truly walkable; most residents drive either way.

Commutes: the Twin Cities average about 24 minutes, among the shortest of major metros. Eden Prairie runs about 25 to 40 minutes to downtown, Maple Grove 30 to 45, and Lakeville 40 to 45 (up to an hour on a bad day). Many employers are now in the suburbs, and the Green Line Extension to Eden Prairie is expected in 2027.

Outdoors: the city's Chain of Lakes is hard to beat, but suburbs offer more total space: Eden Prairie's 1,000-plus acres of parks and 225 miles of trails, Plymouth's new 315-acre Northwest Greenway, Maple Grove's Elm Creek Park Reserve and Lake Minnetonka.

New construction is under 2% of Minneapolis sales but more than half in Rogers, Dayton and Corcoran and about a quarter in Lakeville. For resale, suburban homes draw a wider buyer pool, while downtown condos are the softest segment, some taking over 100 days to sell.

faq.q: Is it cheaper to live in Minneapolis or the suburbs?
faq.a: The city's median price is lower, but you typically get an older home on a smaller lot. For the monthly cost of a nice downtown condo, you can often buy a much larger suburban home, according to Jason.

faq.q: How long is the commute from the suburbs to downtown Minneapolis?
faq.a: About 25 to 40 minutes from Eden Prairie, 30 to 45 from Maple Grove and 40 to 45 from Lakeville in normal traffic, according to the video. The Twin Cities average commute is about 24 minutes.

faq.q: Where can I buy new construction near Minneapolis?
faq.a: Mostly in the suburbs. New construction is under 2% of Minneapolis sales, but more than half of sales in Rogers, Dayton and Corcoran and about a quarter in Lakeville.
